indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.1.1.2: Understand the differences between living things, non-living things, and things which have never been alive
indicator.objective: Describe the differences between living and non-living things

skills.description: State simple differences between living and non-living things
Decide whether a given thing is living or non-living and give a simple reason
Choose the best reason for grouping a thing as living or non-living

misconceptions: Non-living things are the same as dead things.
A car moves, so it is living.
A tree does not move from place to place, so it is non-living.
If something does not eat, it is not living.

questions.stem: Living things grow. Which of these grows?
questions.explanation: A tree is a living thing and it grows. Stones, cars, and cups do not grow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a car grows because it gets bigger when more people enter.

questions.stem: Is a dog living or non-living?
questions.explanation: A dog is a living thing. It eats, grows, breathes, and reproduces.
questions.misconception: Pupils may hesitate if they think of a toy dog.

questions.stem: Why is a stone non-living?
hints: Think about how a stone changes over time.
questions.explanation: A stone is non-living because it does not grow, eat, or breathe.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stones move when they roll, so movement equals life.

questions.stem: Which of these is something living things do that non-living things do not?
questions.explanation: Living things reproduce (make babies or new plants). Non-living things cannot do this.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'move' because they have seen cars move.

questions.stem: Which of these is non-living?
hints: Which one does not eat or grow?
questions.explanation: A chair is a non-living thing. It does not grow, eat, or breathe.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think wooden things are living because they come from trees.

questions.stem: How do living things differ from non-living things in terms of eating?
options: Non-living things eat food, living things do not
Living things eat food, non-living things do not
hints: Do you eat? Does a stone eat?
Living things need food for energy.
questions.explanation: Living things eat food to get energy. Non-living things do not eat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cars 'eat' fuel so they are living.

questions.stem: A car moves. Why is a car not a living thing?
options: It does not grow or make babies
hints: Can a car grow? Can it have baby cars?
questions.explanation: A car is non-living because it cannot grow, eat, breathe, or reproduce, even though it can move.
questions.misconception: Pupils often think movement is the only sign of life.

questions.stem: Kwame has a mango tree, a stone, and a bird. Which group does the mango tree belong to?
questions.explanation: A mango tree is a living thing because it grows, needs water, and makes seeds.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants are non-living because they do not move.

questions.stem: Name one thing that living things can do, but a stone cannot do.
hints: Think about how you change as you get older.
questions.explanation: Living things can grow, eat, and breathe. A stone cannot do any of these.
questions.misconception: Pupils may say 'move' but stones can roll if pushed.

questions.stem: Why do we call a plant a living thing?
hints: What does it need to survive?
questions.explanation: A plant is a living thing because it grows, needs water and air, and reproduces.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants are non-living because they do not move around.

questions.stem: Look at these things: fish, stone, tree, book. Which pair are both living?
hints: A fish swims and a tree grows.
questions.explanation: A fish and a tree are both living things. A stone and a book are non-living.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a book is living because it is made of paper from a tree.

questions.stem: A dead branch is on the ground. Which statement is true?
options: It is non-living because it never lived
It does not grow because it is dead
It is a living thing because it is wood
It will grow into a new tree
hints: Is it still part of a living tree?
questions.explanation: A dead branch was once part of a living tree, but now it is dead and will not grow.
questions.misconception: Pupils often confuse 'dead' with 'non-living' or think wood is always living.

questions.stem: Ama says 'My cup is a living thing because it can hold water.' Is she right? Explain why.

criteria.description: Explains that the cup does not grow, eat, or breathe

questions.explanation: A cup is non-living because it cannot grow, eat, breathe, or reproduce.

questions.stem: Put these into two groups: goat, stone, cup, tree.
answer: living: goat tree, non-living: stone cup
living: goat, tree; non-living: stone, cup
questions.explanation: A goat and a tree are living things. A stone and a cup are non-living things.
questions.misconception: Pupils may struggle to group a plant with an animal as 'living'.

questions.stem: Which of these shows that a living thing is different from a non-living thing?
options: A baby grows into a child
hints: Think about how people change over time.
questions.explanation: A baby growing into a child shows growth, which is a characteristic of living things.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'breaking' as a change, but breaking is not growth.

questions.stem: Why is a moving car NOT considered a living thing?
options: It cannot make its own food or reproduce
hints: Can a car have baby cars?
Living things eat and make babies.
questions.explanation: A car cannot eat, grow, or reproduce, so it is non-living even though it moves.
questions.misconception: Pupils may focus on what makes the car move rather than the characteristics of life.

questions.stem: A boy sees a tall object in the garden. It has green leaves and brown stems. Is it living or non-living?
hints: Leaves and stems are parts of a plant.
questions.explanation: The object is a plant (living thing) because it has leaves and stems.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it is non-living if it does not move.

questions.stem: Write two ways a goat is different from a stone.

criteria.description: States one correct difference (e.g., goat grows, stone does not)
States a second correct difference (e.g., goat eats, stone does not)

hints: What does a goat do that a stone cannot do?
questions.explanation: This tests comparison of living and non-living things.

questions.stem: Tell me why a stone is not a living thing.
questions.explanation: A stone is non-living because it does not grow, eat, or breathe.

questions.stem: Which of these is a thing that has NEVER been alive?
hints: A table was once a tree.
A leaf was once on a plant.
questions.explanation: A stone has never been alive. Wood, leaves, and fish were once alive.
questions.misconception: Pupils often confuse non-living things that come from living things (like wood) with things that have never been alive.
